summary: Classify programs that omit only finitely many inputs using ordered complement markers and a fair finite-stage construction.
abstract: A program can halt on infinitely many inputs while still omitting infinitely many others. Asking whether only finitely many inputs are omitted is a harder classification problem: it is complete for the third existential level of the arithmetical hierarchy. The proof turns candidate enumerable rows into an ordinary program whose missing inputs carry ordered markers. Repeated discoveries in one infinite row keep moving a fixed marker and leave only finitely many omissions. If every row is finite, each finite marker prefix eventually settles and supplies permanent omissions of every finite size. A careful schedule counts each discovery once, even when it is first inspected late. The resulting uniform translation proves the matching lower bound, and complementation classifies programs with infinitely many omitted inputs.
